Why does a gas push on the walls of its container with a steady pressure, and
why do the speeds of its molecules follow one particular curve, when each
molecule only ever meets a wall or a neighbour? Neither the pressure nor the
curve belongs to any molecule. They belong to the many. A model that wants to
reproduce them has to produce them without being told.

An agent-based model has no equation for the whole system. It has many
agents, each following a simple rule that refers only to what is near it, and
it runs them. This lesson builds the smallest such model of physics: a gas of
identical discs in a box. A disc moves in a straight line, bounces off a wall,
and collides elastically with a disc it touches, the collision of the momentum
and collisions lesson. No rule mentions pressure, temperature, or a
distribution of speeds.

The lesson then measures these from the whole. The pressure on the walls is
the impulse the walls gave, per second and per length. The distribution of
speeds is read off the discs. Both can be predicted by kinetic theory, so the
model has something to be checked against: collisions that start from discs of
one speed should produce the Maxwell distribution, and the walls should feel
the pressure of the gas law. The checks are statistical, because the model is
random; the lesson states the tolerance and says what it means. They are
numerical checks of a model against a theory. No real gas is measured here.

## Assumptions

1. **Two dimensions, identical hard discs.** Every disc has the same radius
   and mass, and discs are smooth, so a collision exchanges momentum along
   the line of centres only and nothing spins. In three dimensions the
   speeds follow the three-dimensional Maxwell distribution and the numbers
   below change; the method does not.
2. **Elastic collisions and perfectly reflecting walls.** Kinetic energy
   is conserved by every collision and every bounce. A wall at rest only
   reverses the normal velocity, so it gives momentum to the gas but no
   energy. With dissipation the gas would cool, and there would be no
   temperature to compare.
3. **The gas is dilute.** The area of the discs is a small fraction
   $\varphi$ of the area their centres can reach. Collisions then involve two
   discs at a time, and the first correction to the ideal gas law, the area
   the discs exclude, is enough. This is the first term of a series in
   $\varphi$; the test of the code compares the pressure with this one term
   at the packing fraction used, within the statistical error. A dense gas needs more of
   the series, and a collision of three discs at once is outside the model.
4. **The time step resolves a collision.** The program moves all discs by
   $\Delta t$, then collides the pairs that overlap and approach each other,
   one pair after the other. A disc therefore overlaps another by up to the
   distance it moves in one step, and a collision is placed at the end of the
   step, not at the moment of contact. The step must be small against the
   diameter, or two discs pass through each other. The first worked example
   prints the distance a disc moves in a step as a fraction of the diameter.
5. **The gas has relaxed before it is measured.** The start is not a Maxwell
   distribution. Every disc is first given the same speed in a random
   direction; the mean velocity is then removed, so that the gas has no
   bulk motion, and the velocities are rescaled to the stated kinetic
   energy. Removing the mean velocity changes each speed a little, so the
   discs start in a narrow band of speeds around the stated root-mean-square
   speed. The measurement begins after the collisions have had time to
   change that, and the lesson shows it happening.
6. **The runs are independent, the discs in a run are not.** The discs of one
   run share energy through their collisions, and one disc at successive
   times is correlated with itself. The standard error of a quantity is
   therefore computed from the spread between independent runs started from
   different seeds, never from the number of discs or snapshots.
7. **Randomness is seeded.** A random number generator created from a seed
   makes the start of a run, so a run is a function of its inputs and the
   page is the same at every build. A reader on another machine gets the same
   digits as the page up to the rounding of the floating-point libraries,
   which the displayed precision is chosen to hide.

## Explanation

### From a local rule to a whole

The state of the model is a position and a velocity for each disc. One step
does three things in order:

1. every disc moves, $\mathbf x \leftarrow \mathbf x + \mathbf v\,\Delta t$;
2. a disc that crossed a wall is put back inside and the component of its
   velocity normal to the wall is reversed;
3. every pair of discs that overlap and are still approaching collides
   elastically: the relative velocity along the line of centres reverses,
   the rest is unchanged (`hard_sphere_collision` of the earlier lesson).

The second and third steps are the only places where discs affect anything, and each
involves a disc and its immediate neighbour or wall. The pressure and the
distribution of speeds below are properties of the many, not of any rule.
That is what is meant by *emergent* here: the rules are written once for one
agent, and the quantity is found only by running all of them.

### Pressure

A disc of mass $m$ that bounces off a wall with normal speed $v_n$ gives the
wall the impulse $2 m v_n$. Add the impulses over a time $T$ and divide by the
time and by the length of the wall, $4 L$ for a square of side $L$, and the
result is a force per length, the pressure of a two-dimensional gas.

Kinetic theory predicts the value for point particles. In a short time
$\Delta t$ the discs that hit a wall of length $\ell$ are those that move
towards it and are within $v_n\,\Delta t$ of it. With $n = N/A$ discs per
area, half of them moving towards the wall, the impulse per time and per
length is $\tfrac n2\,\langle v_n \cdot 2 m v_n\rangle = n\,m\,\langle v_n^2\rangle$.
By symmetry $\langle v_n^2\rangle = \tfrac12\langle v^2\rangle$, so the ideal
gas law follows,

$$
P = \frac{N k_B T}{A},
\qquad
k_B T = \tfrac12 m \langle v^2 \rangle,
$$

where $A$ is the area, and the second equation is the definition of the
temperature of a two-dimensional gas: each of the two directions holds
$\tfrac12 k_B T$ of kinetic energy per disc. Discs have an area, so
the centres of $N$ of them are confined to less room than their box suggests,
and the pressure is higher. Kinetic theory writes the pressure of a dilute gas
as a series in the density, $P = n k_B T\,(1 + B_2\,n + \dots)$, with the
second virial coefficient $B_2 = \tfrac12\int (1 - e^{-u/k_B T})\,\mathrm d^2 r$
for a pair of discs with the interaction energy $u$ at the distance $r$ of
their centres. That series is quoted here, not derived. For hard discs of
radius $r$, $u$ is infinite when the centres are closer than $2r$ and zero
beyond, so the integrand is one inside a circle of radius $2r$ and zero
outside, and $B_2 = \tfrac12\pi(2r)^2 = 2\pi r^2$. With $n = N/A$ the first
correction is

$$
P = \frac{N k_B T}{A}\,(1 + 2\varphi),
\qquad
\varphi = \frac{N \pi r^2}{A},
$$

with $\varphi$ the packing fraction. Both $A$ and $L$ here are those of the square that the
centres of the discs can reach, of side $L_\text{box} - 2r$, because a disc
meets a wall when its centre is one radius away.

### The distribution of speeds

When the gas has relaxed, each velocity component of a disc is expected to be
Gaussian with the same variance $\sigma^2 = k_B T / m$, independent of the
other. Then the speed $v = \sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2}$ follows the Rayleigh
distribution, the two-dimensional Maxwell distribution. To see this, write the
joint density of the two components, $\frac{1}{2\pi\sigma^2}
e^{-(v_x^2 + v_y^2)/2\sigma^2}$, in polar coordinates: it depends on the speed
$v$ alone, and the area element is $v\,\mathrm dv\,\mathrm d\theta$, so
integrating over the angle gives the density of the speed,

$$
f(v) = \frac{m v}{k_B T}\exp\!\left(-\frac{m v^2}{2 k_B T}\right),
$$

with $\sigma^2 = k_B T/m$. The temperature fixes the whole curve.

::: {.go-deeper ref="maxwell-boltzmann-2d-relaxation"}
The same curve for particles in a plane, and a picture of a gas of elastic
hard particles that starts away from it and relaxes to it, the experiment of the
first worked example. The lesson derives the curve and does not need the page.
:::

To test the shape without fitting a temperature, use a ratio that does not
depend on it. For Gaussian components $v^2 = v_x^2 + v_y^2$ is exponentially
distributed with mean $2\sigma^2$, and an exponential variable of mean $\mu$
has second moment $2\mu^2$, so $\langle v^2\rangle = 2\sigma^2$ and
$\langle v^4\rangle = 2(2\sigma^2)^2 = 8\sigma^4$. Then

$$
\frac{\langle v^4\rangle}{\langle v^2\rangle^2} = 2,
$$

whatever the temperature. If every disc has the same speed the ratio is one,
which is where the model starts.

### What the tolerance means

A run gives one value of each quantity, and another seed gives another. With
$k$ independent runs, the mean of the values estimates the quantity and the
standard error $s/\sqrt{k}$, with $s$ the sample standard deviation, says how
far the mean is likely to be from the value the model would give for
unlimited runs. A result agrees with theory within $4$ standard errors if
$\lvert \text{mean} - \text{theory}\rvert \le 4\,\text{standard error}$.
Four is a chosen tolerance, not a law. Because $s$ is itself estimated from
only $k = 6$ runs, the discrepancy in standard errors follows Student's $t$
distribution with $k - 1 = 5$ degrees of freedom, whose tails are much wider
than a Gaussian's: chance alone exceeds four standard errors in about one
case in a hundred, where a Gaussian error would do so in one case in fifteen
thousand. A failure is therefore a strong reason to look at the model or the
program, not a proof against them; a repeat with other seeds tells the two
apart. The tests use the same tolerance. It is also a statement about what
the check can see: a model that is wrong by more than four standard errors
is caught, and one that is wrong by less is not.

### Not the LLM agents strand

The agents of this strand and the agents of the LLM agents strand share a
word and little else. Here an agent is a few lines of code with a fixed rule,
it needs no model, no network, and no key, and the same seed gives the same
run. The interest is in what many of them do together. In the LLM agents
strand a single agent is a language model that chooses which experiment
to run, its choices cannot be predicted from code, and the page shows a
recording of them. A model of this strand can be checked against theory; an
LLM agent is checked by replaying what it did.

### The relaxed gas against kinetic theory

Now the measurement. Each of the six seeds runs a gas, relaxes it for
`{python} result["relax"]` s, and measures it for the next
`{python} result["duration"]` s.


```{python}

```

The kinetic energy is the same in every run, because the collisions and bounces
conserve it and every run starts with the same.

[The moment ratio of the relaxed gas agrees with the Maxwell value two within
the tolerance of four standard errors, and the pressure agrees with the virial
prediction that includes the area of the discs.]{.claim
type="numerically-verified" scope="a dilute gas of hard discs in two
dimensions, six seeds, four standard errors" evidence="kinetic-theory-check"}
The ratio is `{python} result["ratio-mean"]` with a standard error of
`{python} result["ratio-error"]` over the six runs, within
`{python} result["ratio-distance"]` standard errors of two.
The pressure is `{python} result["pressure-mean"]` times that of ideal points, and
the prediction with the area of the discs is `{python} result["predicted"]`, a
difference of `{python} result["pressure-distance"]`
standard errors. The ideal gas law alone is off by
`{python} result["ideal-distance"]` standard errors, so the
area of the discs matters and the check can tell the two apart.

## Limits {#limits}

The checks compare two numbers with theory, within the statistical tolerance of
the runs, in a model that was computed.

- **A model checked against a theory, not against a gas.** The data are
  simulated. The result says that the model produces a Maxwell distribution
  and the virial pressure of a dilute gas. It does not say that the model is a
  gas of real molecules: the discs are two-dimensional, smooth, and elastic.
  No experiment is involved, so no claim of this lesson is experimentally
  supported.
- **What the tolerance can see.** A model wrong by more than four standard
  errors is caught, and one wrong by less is not. One moment ratio does not fix
  a distribution: it is a test of the shape, not a proof of it.
- **The time step.** The step resolves a collision only to a fraction of a
  diameter, and a collision is placed at the end of the step.
- **The first rule in isolation.** The checks do not test a single wall
  bounce or collision; unit tests of one bounce and one collision compare the
  outcome with the exact one.
- **Few runs, one density.** Six runs give a standard error that is itself
  uncertain. Only the density of the first example and that of the exercise are
  tried, and a dense gas needs more of the series.

::: {.exercise .self-check}
The moment ratio of the relaxed gas is within the tolerance of two. Does that
show that the speeds follow the Maxwell distribution? What would a failure show?

::: {.solution}
No. The ratio tests one property of the shape, the same for any distribution
whose fourth moment is twice the squared second moment, and it is compared with
two only to within four standard errors of six runs, so a distribution that
differs a little is not caught. The histogram against the curve is a second,
looser look. A failure would be a strong reason to look at the model or the
program, not a proof against them: the discrepancy follows a $t$ distribution
with five degrees of freedom, whose tails are wider than a Gaussian's, and a
repeat with other seeds tells chance and error apart.
:::
:::

## Exercises

::: {.exercise}
**A denser gas.** How many discs of the same radius give a packing
fraction of 5 per cent, and what does the virial correction predict for the
pressure? Run one seed of that gas and compare it with the packing fraction
of the first worked example.

::: {.solution}
The packing fraction is $N \pi r^2 / L_\text{free}^2$, with $L_\text{free}$
the side the centres can reach, so $N = \varphi L_\text{free}^2 / (\pi r^2)$.

```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment.denser_gas)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
result.table("denser-gas")
```

One seed is one run, so its pressure differs from the prediction by about
the spread between the runs of the table above, not by the standard error of
their mean.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
**Same seed, same gas.** Run the gas of seed 0 twice and the gas of seed 1
once, each for half a second. Which of the final speeds agree?

::: {.solution}
The generator is created from the seed, and nothing else in the model is
random, so the same seed gives the same run, bit for bit, and another seed
gives another.
